mcqs.question: A unit test needs to call code that depends on the current wall-clock time. Why is that a good reason to use a test double?
options: Because the real clock is non-deterministic, so the test would pass or fail depending on when it happened to run
Because the real clock is slow to call in a loop
Because clocks always require a network round trip to query
Because test doubles are required for any dependency that isn't a primitive type
mcqs.explanation: The problem with the real clock isn't speed or network access — it's that its value changes from run to run, so assertions written against "now" become flaky. A double lets you fix the time the test sees. Speed and network calls are unrelated to why a clock specifically is risky, and there's no blanket rule about primitive vs non-primitive dependencies.

mcqs.question: A test needs to confirm that `notify()` was called on a dependency exactly once, with specific arguments — the dependency's return value doesn't matter at all. Which test double fits?
options: A dummy, since the return value is unused
A mock, since the interaction itself is what's being verified
A stub, since it only needs to return a canned value
A fake, since it needs realistic behavior
mcqs.explanation: When the thing under test is the call happening with the right arguments — not any resulting value — a mock is the tool built for exactly that: it fails the test if the expected interaction didn't occur. A dummy is never called meaningfully, a stub is about controlling returned values, and a fake is for realistic behavior, neither of which is the point here.

mcqs.question: In the mockist-style test `gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(amount=42.50)`, what is actually being verified?
options: That the checkout function returns a value of 42.50
That the gateway object was constructed correctly
That the gateway's charge method was invoked exactly once with that argument, regardless of what it would have done
That the real payment gateway successfully processed a charge of 42.50
mcqs.explanation: This assertion checks the interaction — that a specific call happened with specific arguments — and says nothing about a return value or about what a real charge call would actually do, since no real gateway is involved. It's also not checking construction, just the one method call.

mcqs.question: A codebase publishes a message to a queue as its only observable side effect of an operation, with no other state to check. Which testing philosophy does this scenario favor?
options: Classicist, because state assertions are always preferable
Neither — this scenario cannot be unit tested at all
Classicist, by using a fake message queue that discards all messages
Mockist, because the interaction itself is the only observable contract available
mcqs.explanation: When a side effect has no other observable trace, verifying the interaction (that publish was called correctly) is the only signal a fast unit test can check — exactly the case mockist-style testing is built for. Preferring state assertions doesn't apply when there's no resulting state to assert on, and a discard-everything fake would make the test unable to check anything.

mcqs.question: A test suite is 100% green, but a refactor that changed a dependency's real return values just broke production. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Over-mocking — the dependency was mocked so thoroughly that no test ever exercised its real, current behavior
The tests weren't run before the change was merged
The CI pipeline has a caching bug returning stale results
The dependency's interface changed in a way that's impossible to test for
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic over-mocking failure mode: every seam is mocked with canned answers, so a real behavior change in a dependency never surfaces because nothing in the suite calls the real thing. It isn't about tests not running or CI caching, and interface changes are entirely testable — that's exactly what an integration test or a well-scoped fake would catch.

mcqs.question: Why is mocking a third-party library's class directly, instead of behind your own adapter interface, considered risky?
options: It makes the test run noticeably slower
Third-party classes cannot technically be mocked by most frameworks
Your tests encode assumptions about the library's internal contract, so a library upgrade can break production while the mocked tests keep passing unaware
It violates most licensing agreements for third-party libraries
mcqs.explanation: A test that mocks a library type directly bakes in that version's method names and shapes; if the library changes, production breaks but the tests — still mocking the old shape — never notice. It has nothing to do with runtime speed, mockability limits, or licensing.
